prediction.evidence_summary: Assuming that higher group‑signal availability provides richer feedback for the fixed‑trainer RL policy and that higher admission cost reflects higher‑quality data, the environment with both high signals and high admission cost (C01) is expected to achieve the highest held‑out pass@1, followed by high‑signal low‑cost (C02), low‑signal high‑cost (C03), and low‑signal low‑cost (C04). The lack of direct outcome data limits confidence.

Cross‑study data show that interventions with higher signal availability consistently achieve higher normalized utility, while lower admission cost (or less restrictive selection) also tends to improve performance. Applying this pattern to the four candidates (high/low signal × high/low admission cost) suggests the ordering C02 (high signal, low cost) > C01 (high signal, high cost) > C04 (low signal, low cost) > C03 (low signal, high cost).

C01 leads on reward per token (rho), effective prompt coverage, mixed-group rate and admission rate, suggesting the highest heldout_pass_at_1. C02 is second with top prompt coverage and mixed-group rate but lower admission and reward. C03 has high admission but very low coverage and reward, placing it third. C04 scores lowest across all key metrics, giving it the lowest expected utility.

Historical panels show that higher signal coverage, mixed‑group diversity, reward density (rho per token) and baseline success rate tend to increase downstream utility, while higher admission_rate reflects higher cost and reduces utility. Scoring each candidate with a weighted sum of normalized effective_prompt_coverage, mixed_group_rate, rho_per_million_generated_tokens, starting_success_rate (positive) and admission_rate (negative) yields C01 highest, then C02, then C04, then C03.

High group-signal availability tends to improve mathematical reasoning performance, while lower admission cost reduces resource constraints and enables more models to be admitted, increasing ensemble diversity. Consequently, the environment with high signals and low admission cost (C02) is expected to achieve the highest heldout_pass_at_1, followed by high signals with high cost (C01), low signals with low cost (C04), and finally low signals with high cost (C03).

Across all provided panels, interventions with higher signal/coverage and lower data cost consistently achieved higher within‑panel normalized utilities (e.g., 'all data', 'length 50', 'diversity only retain' vs. random or low‑signal variants). Interpreting 'group‑signal availability' as signal/coverage and 'admission cost' as data cost, the combination of high signal and low cost (C02) is expected to yield the highest held‑out pass@1, followed by high signal/high cost (C01). Low signal/low cost (C04) should outperform low signal/high cost (C03). This ordering informs the assigned scores and ranking.

C01 exhibits the strongest values across all performance proxies (effective_prompt_coverage, starting_success_rate, reward per token, and mixed_group_rate), which dominate the expected heldout_pass_at_1. Its higher admission cost is outweighed by these gains. C02 retains a high mixed_group_rate while having a lower admission cost, giving it the second‑best utility. C03 and C04 have low mixed_group_rates and weaker performance metrics, resulting in lower expected pass@1 despite their lower costs.

C01 exhibits the highest effective_prompt_coverage, admission_rate, mixed_group_rate, reward density (rho per million tokens) and starting_success_rate while using relatively few generated tokens—attributes that historically align with higher utility. C02 ranks second with strong coverage and mixed‑group rate but lower admission and higher token usage. C03 has a high admission_rate but low coverage, mixed‑group rate, and reward density, reducing its expected utility. C04 scores lowest across all measured dimensions, indicating the least expected downstream benefit.

Environments with high group-signal availability tend to improve mathematical reasoning performance, while lower admission cost reduces overhead and increases net utility. All candidates share the same 'mixed' characteristic, so the primary differentiators are signal availability (high vs low) and admission cost (low vs high). Combining these factors yields the ordering: C02 (high signal, low cost) > C01 (high signal, high cost) > C04 (low signal, low cost) > C03 (low signal, high cost).

Across the provided cross‑study history, environments that offer high group‑signal availability (e.g., all‑data, curated or diversity‑focused selections) consistently achieve the highest normalized utilities, while low‑signal or random selections perform poorly. The studies do not vary admission cost, so we have no direct evidence that high vs. low cost changes utility. Consequently we rank the two high‑signal candidates (C01 and C02) above the two low‑signal candidates (C04 and C03), treating the cost dimension as neutral. The confidence reflects strong evidence for the signal dimension and uncertainty about the cost dimension.
